Before readout, the direct-sum amplitude map is an isometry retaining coherent quantum output sectors. A classically recorded instrument is obtained by the specified dephasing or measurement of those sectors (and time bins, when used). For an exact-time classical record the output is an integrable trace-class-valued kernel on the null/flag atoms and [0, T], with norm ∑︁ c ∥ωc∥1 + ∫︁T 0 ∥ω(t)∥1dt. It is not a trace-class diagonal density operator on the coherent temporal L2 space. Finite time bins give ordinary cq direct sums. These channels share the displayed effects but are not identical channels; their dilation and storage costs must be counted separately. This uses the stipulated ordinary quantum probability law; it does not derive that law. Only the terminal flags are conclusive. They are committed after the active coupling is switched off. Before that time, flag amplitudes can coherently return to the source, so no promise of an earlier immutable event is made. After decoupling, later controls act on other systems and leave all flag and loss modes untouched; the final records then persist. Reading or dephasing the flags during the active pulse is a different physical model.
